sections.html:
Mobile is the Mobile County seat, at the head of Mobile Bay on Alabama's Gulf Coast, and the state's only deep water port city. Of the city's 180.07 square miles, 22.5 percent is water. The land climbs from 10 feet on Water Street downtown to 211 feet at the Mobile Regional Airport, and low blocks by the water behave very differently from the higher ground west of downtown.

Residents numbered 187,041 in 2020. An annexation of land west of the city in July 2023 lifted the count to 204,689, and the 2025 estimate is 200,824. Those counts came from 77,772 households with a median age of 37.3, and 17.3 percent of residents were 65 or older. Neighborhoods differ widely in age, ownership and housing type across 139 square miles of land, so a house's value depends on its exact location.

sections.h2: How buyers read a Mobile address
sections.html:
Location carries more weight here than in many cities. A house near the bay or in a low area faces different flood and insurance questions than one on higher ground west of downtown, and buyers check both. Say clearly where yours sits and whether it has ever taken in water.

Newer pockets that came into the city through the 2023 annexation may have different services than older streets. Ask the city which rules apply to your address, and tell buyers what you learn.

sections.h2: Hurricanes, rain and what buyers check
sections.html:
Mobile averages 66.3 inches of rain a year, and hurricanes, storm surge and tornadoes are part of its history. Sellers often face roof, flood and water damage questions.

  • Hurricane Frederic, Category 3, struck on September 12, 1979.
  • Katrina's storm surge reached 11.45 feet in 2005.
  • Hurricane Sally hit in 2020, followed a month later by Zeta, a Category 3.
  • A tornado on December 25, 2012 damaged at least 100 structures in Midtown.

Heavy rain and humidity also feed mold and rot in older homes. Inspectors for buyers go over roofs, crawl spaces and drainage with care. Snow is rare, but it struck on January 21, 2025 with accumulations up to 8.5 inches, and pipes and roofs built for a mild climate can be strained by an event like that. A cash buyer can price these findings in without waiting on a lender's repair demands.

Historic neighborhoods include Ashland Place, Campground, Church Street East, De Tonti Square, Leinkauf, Lower Dauphin Street, Midtown, Oakleigh Garden, Old Dauphin Way, Spring Hill and Toulminville. Styles include shotgun houses, Colonial Revival, Tudor Revival and Spanish Colonial Revival.

Older houses in these areas can have original wood windows, old wiring and settled foundations. Before telling a buyer they can change the exterior, call the city planning office and ask if a district review applies. Sellers near downtown may also want to plan showings around the Carnival calendar.

Property tax is handled by the Mobile County Revenue Commission, whose offices are closed on Wednesdays, so plan your visit for another day. Bills are due October 1, and a balance still open after December 31 is delinquent.

A bill follows the owner of record, so check that this year's tax shows up on the closing statement. If you sell mid-year, the bill is normally divided between you and the buyer.

On the deed itself, Alabama Code 40-22-1 sets a recording tax of 50 cents per $500 of value, and proof of the real price is filed with it.

A buyer who accepts the condition can take a storm-damaged house as-is. Name the damage you know about, and clear title and tax items before closing. Keep any insurance claim papers, contractor estimates and permits. They help a buyer judge what has already been fixed.

Many buyers want the flood zone and the insurance record, so have the policy, the premium and any claim history handy.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Mobile
sections.html:
A cash sale starts with an offer, then a title search, a signed contract and a closing at a title or law office. The deed is recorded afterward and the tax is paid on recording.

StepWhat happensWho handles it
OfferYou describe the house and timing and receive a priceYou and the buyer
Title searchLiens, tax and ownership are checkedTitle or law office
ContractTerms and closing date are agreedYou and the buyer
ClosingDeed signed and recorded, tax paidClosing office

Repairs can be left to the buyer. Title work still applies to every sale, and so does paying tax owed.

sections.h2: If a mortgage or tax is still owed
sections.html:
A debt against the house does not end a sale. Your lender states the payoff, the closing office pays it out of the proceeds, and the lien lifts as the deed changes hands. Overdue property tax follows the same path.

Request the payoff and the tax balance before you accept anything. With both in front of you, you can see what you would take home and judge whether a quick sale is worth it.

After the July 2023 annexation west of the city, check whether your parcel falls inside city limits when you look into taxes and services. The Revenue Commission and the city can tell you which rules apply to your address.

sections.h2: Selling an inherited or rental house in Mobile
sections.html:
Inherited houses and rentals are common cash sales in Mobile. Heirs often live elsewhere, and a house that sits empty through hurricane season picks up damage and worry. If the owner has died, the first step is to find out who has authority to sign, which a probate attorney can confirm.

For a rental, say whether the tenant is staying and bring the lease and deposit records. Check the lease for notice terms, and give any notices it requires before you pick a closing date.

Whatever the situation, gather the deed, the newest tax bill and any lender statement first, so a title office can begin its search at once.

Once you accept an offer, the title search usually takes the most time. Liens, tax balances and heirs with a claim are the items that slow it. A clean file can close in a matter of weeks, and a house with problems needs longer. If you have a firm date, say so at the start so everyone works toward it.

On closing day you sign the deed and the settlement statement, any lender is paid off, and the deed is filed. Your proceeds arrive once the filing is done.

Reasons owners sell include storm damage, inheritance, tenants and a move. Medical and university jobs bring steady turnover of staff, residents and students, and some households sell quickly when a contract ends or a new position starts elsewhere.

sections.h2: What to bring to the closing
sections.html: Bring a photo ID, the deed or trust papers, a payoff letter from any lender, and all keys and garage openers. If heirs share the house, each one signs. The closing office will tell you if it needs anything else.

faqs.q: What is the population of Mobile, AL?
faqs.a: The 2025 estimate is 200,824 residents. The 2020 census counted 187,041, and a 2023 annexation added land west of the city.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Mobile, Alabama?
faqs.a: Bills are due October 1, and unpaid ones are delinquent after December 31.

faqs.q: Is Mobile at risk from hurricanes?
faqs.a: Yes. Frederic in 1979, Katrina in 2005, Sally and Zeta in 2020 all affected the city. Storm surge and wind damage are common reasons for repairs before a sale.

faqs.q: What is the Alabama deed tax?
faqs.a: The state charges fifty cents on every $500 of value conveyed, a rule in Alabama Code 40-22-1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a storm damaged house in Mobile?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer who accepts the condition can purchase it as-is. Disclose the damage you know about and clear title and tax items before closing.
